card.hook: You've climbed a mountain to get here, and the first thing that hits you is a 24-metre gold chedi glowing like it's got its own power supply. Take a breath, then take the photo.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 10 m south-west of the gold chedi at Wat Phra That Doi Suthep, and face north-east. It's less than a minute on foot from the middle of the complex.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the chedi and the main buildings. Go 0.5x in the courtyard or when you're too close to fit the tall chedi in. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for roof details, carved figures and the city view.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the chedi on a vertical line so the spire stays straight, then tap the gold and drag the slider a little darker so the gilding keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Early morning is usually calmer and often gives a clearer view over the city. Late afternoon can put a warm glow on the gold.
card.selfie_here: Head to the upper terrace in front of the gilded chedi, turn your back to it and use the front camera so the chedi fills the frame behind you. For a different shot, try the Naga staircase: stand on a step between the serpent railings with the temple above you, which is less crowded early in the morning.
card.ask_someone: At the roadside 'view of the chedi' stop on the way up, ask someone to shoot you at the railing with the temple below you, and keep well clear of the traffic because there's no parking or facilities there.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working place of worship, so dress modestly and take your shoes off where asked. Flash isn't allowed inside the main ubosot, and entry rules may apply, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find a doorway, shrine roof or statue to use as a frame, and get the gold chedi into the shot without any strangers' faces in it.
card.good_to_know: Wat Phra That Doi Suthep is a Theravada Buddhist temple about 15 km from Chiang Mai, sitting 1,073 metres above sea level. Tradition says it was founded in 1383, when the first stupa was built. You'll also hear the story of a white elephant carrying a relic up the mountain.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 10 m south-west of the gold chedi at Wat Phra That Doi Suthep, and face north-east. It's less than a minute on foot from the middle of the complex.

Opening hours also conflict (6 AM to 6 PM per Tour Guide; a 5 AM opening per Unearth the Voyage). Step counts vary (306 vs 309). No page I found gives a specific spot where a passer-by should stand to photograph a visitor with the whole temple in frame, so the roadside stop is the nearest match and is only described as a viewing point over the temple. No selfie-stick rule was found for this temple; the selfie-stick and tripod rules I found are for Bangkok and Japan and do not apply here. Several sources are 2-3 years old. One guide notes that official photographers on site offer to take chedi photos for visitors, which is a paid service rather than a passer-by option.

card.hook: Picture a lane of stalls glowing under string lights and neon signs, with a crowd drifting past and a live band warming up nearby. After dark, the Night Bazaar hands you colour and movement without you doing a thing.
card.stand_here: Start at Kalare Night Bazaar, about 150 m south of the subject, and face north. The main stretch is about 2 minutes on foot from the icon, so just follow the lit stalls along Chang Khlan Road.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x to fit the stalls, lights and crowd in one frame. In the narrow stall lane, switch to zoom 0.5x so the lights overhead fit in. Try zoom 2x or more (depending on your phone) for lanterns or the band on stage.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the scene, then slide the brightness a little darker so the lights keep their colour instead of turning white.
card.best_time: Around 8 PM is the sweet spot, when the live band plays and the string lights are on. Stall lights on the main street come on about 30 minutes after sunset.
card.selfie_here: Head to the north entrance of Changklan Road and turn your back on the lantern-lit stalls, then use the front camera at 0.5x so the lights and neon signs fill the frame behind you. For a different backdrop, try the raised walkway beside the Kalare building, with the food court and its live band behind you.
card.ask_someone: Stand in front of the Kalare Night Bazaar main entrance on Chiangklan Road, by its colourful sign, and ask your helper to stand back from the gate so the whole entrance fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is freely allowed at the Night Bazaar, but ask before taking close-ups of stallholders. The food court and any walkway may have their own rules, so check the official site. Keep your phone strap on and a hand free in the crowd, as one guide lists pickpocket warnings.
card.challenge: Find a frame with three different colours of light in it, then add your best 'I'm just browsing' face.
card.good_to_know: The Night Bazaar sits just east of the old city moat, between the moat and the Ping River. It began under Chinese merchants, then grew as more commercial buildings went up. Today it has many owners, most of them Thai, and it's known for handicrafts and portrait paintings.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start at Kalare Night Bazaar, about 150 m south of the subject, and face north. The main stretch is about 2 minutes on foot from the icon, so just follow the lit stalls along Chang Khlan Road.

card.hook: This chedi lost its top 30 m to an earthquake in 1545, and honestly it looks better for it. After dark the floodlights pick out every crack and ledge in the old brick.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, which sits right at the subject inside the temple grounds. Walk round to the east face of the chedi and face it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole chedi in. If you're close and it won't fit, drop to 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for brick texture and carved details.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest bit of brick, then slide the brightness down a touch so the floodlit surface doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Come after dark, when the floodlights light up the brickwork, or in the first hour after sunrise, when morning light hits the east face. Both are lovely, and both are quieter than midday.
card.selfie_here: Stand in front of the main chedi's base so the damaged stupa fills the view behind you. Or pose beside one of the elephant figures around the lower base. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the chedi over your shoulder. These spots come from one visitor guide, so treat them as approximate.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at a corner of the chedi platform (no one says which corner, so shuffle around until you both fit) while you stand in front of the chedi, so you and the whole chedi land in one frame.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working temple, so keep your distance from monks and worshippers and don't photograph them. Photos are fine at the chedi and grounds, but not inside the Sao Inthakhin city pillar shrine, where posted signs are enforced. Climb the accessible steps for close-ups, but respect roped-off areas and signs.
card.challenge: Find the elephant figures around the base, then try to get one elephant and the broken top of the chedi in the same shot.
card.good_to_know: Building began in the 14th century, and by the mid-15th century the chedi stood about 82 m high with a base some 54 m across, the largest building in all of Lan Na. The Emerald Buddha was installed in the east niche in 1468, and a black jade copy sits there now. The chedi was partly reconstructed in the early 1990s.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, which sits right at the subject inside the temple grounds. Walk round to the east face of the chedi and face it.

card.hook: Picture a gold bell-shaped chedi glowing against a blue sky, with a ring of stone elephants holding up its base. That's the shot everyone comes to Wat Phra Singh for, and it's a good one.
card.stand_here: Walk into the grounds of Wat Phra Singh to the phone icon on the map, at the centre of the compound and right at the subject itself. Face north toward the main chedi and let the sky fill the top of your frame.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole chedi in. Then try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) for the elephant reliefs and the gold detail. Save 0.5x for the long temple roofs or Ho Trai, and keep your phone level so the lines don't lean.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the gold part of the chedi, then slide the brightness down a little so the gold keeps its colour instead of going pale, and turn the flash off.
card.best_time: Late afternoon, about 4:30 to 5:30 pm, when the low sun warms up the gold. Early morning (about 7:30 to 9:00) is also worth a try. Songkran in April makes the grounds very crowded.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone offers it, and hold the phone slightly low so the golden landmark sits over your shoulder. Take a few, because the sky looks great behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: This is an active place of worship. The grounds are free, but foreign visitors are asked for a small donation to enter Viharn Lai Kham, so check the official site before you go. Photography inside Viharn Lai Kham is restricted, flash is banned, and Ho Trai is kept locked, so plan on exterior shots only.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines, put the chedi on one side, and keep the elephants in the bottom third with a big slice of sky above. Bonus points if the gold looks warm!
card.good_to_know: King Phayu of Lan Na founded Wat Phra Singh in 1345 to hold his father's ashes. It later became home to the revered Phra Buddha Sihing image. The main hall, Viharn Luang, dates from 1924 and is 56 metres long, with a layered Lanna-style teak roof.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk into the grounds of Wat Phra Singh to the phone icon on the map, at the centre of the compound and right at the subject itself. Face north toward the main chedi and let the sky fill the top of your frame.

card.hook: Picture warm red brick glowing against an open square, with a flock of pigeons who clearly think the place belongs to them. That's Tha Phae Gate, and it looks good even on a quick stop.
card.stand_here: Stand in Tha Phae Square, inside the plaza, and face the gate; from the nearest point, the gate is to the north-west, about 2 minutes on foot. If you can, drift to the right-hand side of the plaza, where one guide says the light is nicer.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole gate and the plaza in one frame. Crouch low and try 0.5x to make the pigeons big in the foreground, then go to 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the brickwork, the roofline and the wooden door.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brick wall, then drag the brightness slider down a little so the sky stays blue and the brick looks rich.
card.best_time: Go between 6 and 8 am, when low side-light rakes across the brick and the square is at its calmest. After dark, walk to Tha Phae Road for the lit-up gate against a blue sky, and use night mode with your phone held steady against your body or a wall.
card.selfie_here: Try the bridge over the moat on the outer side of the gate. Use the front camera, keep the gate behind you, and let the arch and red brick fill the frame over your shoulder (check where the bridge sits on the map first). The inner plaza works too, with the gate behind you and the pigeons adding some life.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the open plaza facing the gate, ideally on the right-hand side for the better light, while you pose in front of the arch.
card.rules_and_safety: Please don't feed the pigeons, as feeding them may be illegal. Don't lean on or climb the brick walls. On Sunday evenings the market crowds can fill the square, so arrive early for a clear frame.
card.challenge: Crouch down to knee height, turn on gridlines and get the whole gate in the frame with at least one pigeon in the foreground looking like the star.
card.good_to_know: A gate has stood here since Chiang Mai was founded in 1296, but what you see today is a reconstruction from the mid-1980s. It's the only gate of the old inner wall that still has its complete wooden doors. The square hosts festivals like Yi Peng and Songkran, and the Sunday Walking Street Market starts here.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Tha Phae Square, inside the plaza, and face the gate; from the nearest point, the gate is to the north-west, about 2 minutes on foot. If you can, drift to the right-hand side of the plaza, where one guide says the light is nicer.

card.hook: Most people head straight for the tunnels, but the best quiet picture here is a wooden platform poking out over a lake, where every tree gets a twin in the water.
card.stand_here: Walk to the wooden platform over the lake in the southern part of the compound, right where the phone icon sits on the map. Face across the still water toward the trees and the small chedi on the far bank.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the lake, the reflection and the far bank all fit naturally. If the little chedi looks too far away, try 2x, and use 0.5x only if you want the platform planks in the foreground. Keep the horizon level.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the far bank, then slide the brightness down a touch so the sky doesn't wash out and the reflection stays rich.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is usually best, when the water tends to be calmer and the light softer. Skip windy moments, because ripples break up the reflection.
card.selfie_here: Try it on the small wooden platform over the lake: use the front camera and turn so the water, trees and small chedi are behind you. At the arched brick entrance to the tunnels, the daylight through the arch makes a glowing backdrop, so tap your face so you don't turn into a silhouette.
card.rules_and_safety: Skip the flash near Buddha images and the fragile murals, and drones aren't allowed in the forest reserve. This is a working temple, so dress modestly and ask before photographing monks or meditators. Watch your step, as stones can be slippery after rain.
card.challenge: Get the reflection so crisp that a friend has to turn your phone upside down to work out which half is the real one.
card.good_to_know: Wat Umong is about 700 years old and was founded by King Mangrai for monks invited from Sri Lanka. King Kue Na later restored the stupa and added the walking tunnels it's known for. After a long period of abandonment, it became a meditation centre in 1949.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk to the wooden platform over the lake in the southern part of the compound, right where the phone icon sits on the map. Face across the still water toward the trees and the small chedi on the far bank.

card.hook: Fifteen elephants are trying to walk out of a wall, and they've been at it for a very long time. That's the picture you're here for, but the gate is where the visit starts.
card.stand_here: Stand on Ratchaphakhinai Road, right in front of the main gate of Wat Chiang Man, and look south into the compound. You'll see the main hall and the grounds ahead of you, which makes a good opening shot for your set.
card.zoom: Use 1x for the gate view. Switch to 0.5x inside the courtyard when you're close to the chedi, then try 2x or more (depends on your phone) for the gilded spire and the elephant details.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the gilded spire, then slide the brightness down a little so the gold keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Pick a moment when the gate area is clear of parked vehicles, because they can block the view on the right. Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the stucco and gold than the middle of the day.
card.selfie_here: Stand in the courtyard a few steps in front of the elephant chedi, so the tiers of elephants are behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a little low, and let the elephants and the spire fill the space over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the far left corner of the courtyard while you stand in front of the chedi, so they can catch the full curve of the elephant row with the spire rising behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working temple, so dress modestly. Photos are fine in the grounds, but skip flash, ask before photographing monks, don't take photos inside the main halls with the Buddha images, and don't stand on the chedi.
card.challenge: Get down low by the Chedi Chang Lom and make those elephants look like they're marching straight out of the wall.
card.good_to_know: King Mangrai built Wat Chiang Man in 1297, and it's described as the first temple of Chiang Mai. The Chedi Chang Lom is the oldest structure in the complex. The front halves of 15 life-sized brick-and-stucco elephants come out of its second level, as if carrying the upper chedi on their backs.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Ratchaphakhinai Road, right in front of the main gate of Wat Chiang Man, and look south into the compound. You'll see the main hall and the grounds ahead of you, which makes a good opening shot for your set.

card.hook: Crouch down in the courtyard and a 17-metre seated Buddha suddenly towers over you against the sky. It's a great excuse to get your knees dirty.
card.stand_here: Stand in the temple courtyard in front of the big seated Buddha, right where the phone icon sits on the map. Face the Buddha and hold your phone low, tilted up.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x and keep the phone low so the Buddha fills the frame. If he won't fit, step to zoom 0.5x. Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) is good for the smaller Buddha and the temple details at the edges.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the Buddha, then slide the brightness down a little so the sky stays blue and the gold keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, when the shadows are softer. Around sunset the golden chedi catches warm light, and the Naga-lined steps make a nice leading line.
card.selfie_here: Try the area near the golden chedi, which one sunset guide says has a fantastic perspective. Use the front camera at 0.5x and see if you can fit the golden pagoda over your shoulder. The Doikham Panorama View Point near the far end of the temple grounds is another one reviewers like for photos of themselves.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the foot of the Naga staircase while you stand on the steps, so the temple rises above you.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working place of worship, so dress modestly and keep clear of people praying at the shrines. Avoid flash in sacred spaces and follow any posted photo restrictions. Drones are generally not permitted, and kids need an adult close by on the stairs and around worship areas.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the Buddha's face sits on the top gridline, then one where you look as tiny as possible next to him.
card.good_to_know: Temple records say Wat Phra That Doi Kham was founded in 687 AD, and its name means 'Temple of the Golden Mountain's Relic'. It's known for a very old chedi, said to be around 1,300 years old, and a sacred relic of the Buddha's hair. The old chedi collapsed after heavy rain in 1966, and a community restoration began. There's also a 19-metre statue of Thao Wessuwan on site.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the temple courtyard in front of the big seated Buddha, right where the phone icon sits on the map. Face the Buddha and hold your phone low, tilted up.

card.hook: Picture dried fruit piled high, northern sausages, chilli pastes and a hand reaching for a bag of snacks, all within a few steps of each other. That's Warorot Market, and it's much easier to photograph in small scenes than as one big view.
card.stand_here: Go to Talat Warorot and stand on the second-floor open balcony overlooking the central hall, then point your phone down at the stalls, vendors and shoppers below. After a few wide shots, walk south-east to the market itself for your close-ups, and step to the side of the main aisles.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for most stall and walkway shots, and drop to 0.5x in tight alleys to fit the whole scene in. For food, flowers and fabrics, try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) so you don't crowd anyone.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the stall you want on the screen, then slide the brightness down a little so bright signs and sunny gaps don't wash out the colours.
card.best_time: Earlier in the day is a good bet, as it's likely to be livelier with softer light. Check the official site or ask locally for current opening times.
card.selfie_here: Try the open footbridge between the two market buildings, above Wichayanon Road. A travel guide calls it an excellent photo opportunity. Use the front camera, hold it a little out and up, and tilt it so the market buildings squeeze in. For a more colourful backdrop, try the flower stalls along the Ping River side at the back of the market, which guides call very photogenic.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally tolerated away from food-preparation areas, but ask before taking a close photo of a vendor. Keep moving in busy aisles so you don't block the flow, and check the official site for current opening times and any rules.
card.challenge: Find the most colourful row of goods you can, then add one friendly hand reaching in for the perfect snack photo.
card.good_to_know: Locals call Warorot Market Kad Luang, or the "Big Market", and it's regarded as the largest and best-known market in northern Thailand. The site was once used for funeral ceremonies of Chiang Mai's rulers, until Princess Dara Rasmi turned it into a market in 1910. Look for the alley called Trok Lao Zhou, which is linked with Chinese and Hmong traders and is a good place to spot handicrafts.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Go to Talat Warorot and stand on the second-floor open balcony overlooking the central hall, then point your phone down at the stalls, vendors and shoppers below. After a few wide shots, walk south-east to the market itself for your close-ups, and step to the side of the main aisles.

card.hook: Picture a whole field of little white spires poking up at the sky, while the big gold chedi waits politely behind your back. That's Wat Suan Dok's royal chedi field, and it's a bit magical.
card.stand_here: Head for the white chedi field in the north-western part of the temple grounds and stand at its west edge, right at the phone icon on the map. Face east, so the white spires fill the top of your photo.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole field of white chedis in. Try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a group of spires, and use 0.5x only for the assembly hall gable when you can't step back far enough.
card.make_it_pop: White walls can fool your phone, so tap a white chedi and slide the brightness down a little to keep the detail in the stone.
card.best_time: Come around 17:30, when the low sun lights the white chedis from the front and makes them glow. The exact light changes with the time of year, so check where it falls when you get there.
card.selfie_here: Stand at the west edge of the royal cemetery field with the big golden chedi directly behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a little low, and let the gold tower rise over your shoulder (0.5x helps fit more in).
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are generally fine, but skip them during prayer times or in restricted areas, and ask before photographing people. It's an active temple, so dress modestly and be discreet inside the buildings. The white surfaces can blind you in midday sun, so come earlier or later in the day.
card.challenge: Crouch down until the nearest white chedis overlap the ones behind them, then see if you can make a 'forest' of spires out of the field.
card.good_to_know: The gold main chedi is 48 metres tall and bell-shaped, in a Sri Lankan style. King Kue Na of Lanna founded the temple in 1370 on his flower garden, which is why it's called the 'flower garden temple'. The white chedis hold the ashes of Chiang Mai's royal family. Some chedis near the golden one have had restoration work, so you might see scaffolding.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the white chedi field in the north-western part of the temple grounds and stand at its west edge, right at the phone icon on the map. Face east, so the white spires fill the top of your photo.

card.hook: Picture a zoo day where you pause for a breather and the view is calm water with green hills stacked up behind it. That's Huay Kaew Lake, and pedal boats are sometimes moored at the edge, which adds a bit of life.
card.stand_here: Stand on the shore of Huay Kaew Lake, inside the zoo grounds. The middle of the zoo lies about 1.1 km (roughly 1138 m) to the west of the lake, so face the water and the wooded hills behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the lake, hills and sky together. Try zoom 0.5x if you want more shoreline, or zoom 2x-5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the hillside or the pedal boats.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the water's edge on the lower line, and keep the phone level so the lake looks flat and calm.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the water and hills. The zoo is often quieter early in the day too.
card.selfie_here: Try the central lake shore: use the front camera and stand with the wooded hillside behind you. The main entrance on Huay Kaew Road is another spot, with the gate over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: At the main gate on Huay Kaew Road, stand with the entrance behind you and ask a passer-by to take the photo facing you.
card.rules_and_safety: The lake is inside the paid zoo grounds, so you need a ticket. Photography is free throughout the zoo, but flash isn't allowed in the panda house. Skip flash in animal enclosures so you don't distress the animals.
card.challenge: Get one picture where the water's edge sits on the lower gridline and a moored boat (if there is one) sneaks into the corner.
card.good_to_know: The zoo covers about 200 acres (81 ha) at the foot of Doi Suthep and opened as the province's official zoo in 1977. A smaller animal collection first welcomed visitors in 1957. Today it shows around 400 species and has a 133-metre aquarium tunnel, opened in 2008 and billed as the world's longest.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the shore of Huay Kaew Lake, inside the zoo grounds. The middle of the zoo lies about 1.1 km (roughly 1138 m) to the west of the lake, so face the water and the wooded hills behind it.

card.hook: Three bronze kings, a big open square and nobody telling you to hurry: this might be the easiest 'get everyone in the shot' spot in Chiang Mai. You can step back and fit the whole group in without craning your neck.
card.stand_here: Stand on the open paving in Anusawari Sam Kasat (Three Kings Monument square), on the side facing the bronze figures. Walk westward from the centre of Chiang Mai and the statues will be directly ahead of you, so face west.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to catch all three kings with some of the square around them. Then try zoom 2x to bring the figures closer. Use 0.5x only if you walk right up to the monument and want the open space in the shot too.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the group in the centre with the base near the lower third line, and keep the phone level so the kings don't look like they're leaning.
card.best_time: Morning is a good choice, because the sun is behind you as you face west. Late afternoon puts the sun behind the monument, so check your screen and tap the statues, then slide darker or brighter until you can see their details.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie on the open paving directly in front of the bronze statues, clear of anyone making offerings at the base. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and tilt up a little so the kings sit over your shoulder. The softest light is 06:00-08:00 and 17:00-19:00, which is kinder to faces than midday glare.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the middle of the square, back from the statues, while you stand on the paving in front of the kings, so the monument and the old-city setting both fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photograph from the square, not from the base, and don't climb or sit on the monument. Respect people making offerings: don't move anything or block worshippers for a shot. Don't copy the kings' poses, like horseback or royal gestures, as that can seem disrespectful. Ask before photographing people up close, and keep children away from the kerb on the shaded north side of the square.
card.challenge: Get one shot of all three kings with no strangers in front of them. Wait a moment, take a few tries, and call it patience.
card.good_to_know: The monument honours Phaya Mangrai, Pho Khun Ramkhamhaeng and Phaya Ngammueang, remembered as the founders of the Lanna Kingdom. It marks the founding of Chiang Mai in 1296. National artist Kaimook Chuto designed and cast it, finishing in 1983 and opening it in 1984, and the figures are about 2.7 metres high.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the open paving in Anusawari Sam Kasat (Three Kings Monument square), on the side facing the bronze figures. Walk westward from the centre of Chiang Mai and the statues will be directly ahead of you, so face west.

card.hook: Most temple halls don't have a past as somebody's house, but this one does. Wat Phan Tao's teak hall was once a royal residence, and it has a glass-decorated carved peacock over the door to show for it.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, in the courtyard behind the hall, next to the golden chedi. Face the chedi so its ring of small spires and the red-fenced shrines fill the view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the chedi and its little spires. Go to zoom 0.5x for the whole courtyard, but keep the chedi in the middle so the edges don't stretch it. Try zoom 2x to 5x to pick out the gilded top.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the golden chedi, then slide it a little darker so the gold keeps its detail against the sky.
card.best_time: Go around sunrise or sunset, when the light is low and warm. The chedi glows and the dark teak looks richer too. If you come during Yi Peng (usually November), arrive early because the pond and lantern views get crowded.
card.selfie_here: Head to the garden side of the pond beside the hall, where a Buddha sits on a rock under a Bodhi tree. Use the front camera and put the wooden hall over your shoulder. Zoom 0.5x helps fit more in. One blog says the pond may be gone after remodelling, so check when you arrive.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the garden pond edge facing the hall and the stupa, so they catch both in one shot, with you posing in front of the hall.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are generally fine in the grounds and outside the buildings, but check for signs before shooting inside the hall, and don't point your phone at people who are praying. Dogs roam freely in the compound, so take care if you're wary of them.
card.challenge: Walk a full circuit of the grounds before you shoot anything, then find the glass peacock above the door and see if you can spot a leafy branch to tuck into a corner of your frame.
card.good_to_know: The name means 'temple of a thousand furnaces', a nod to the hearths once used to cast Buddha images. The teak hall was moved here in 1876 and is 21 metres long and 14 metres high. The hall has been closed for repairs in the past, so check the notices on site.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, in the courtyard behind the hall, next to the golden chedi. Face the chedi so its ring of small spires and the red-fenced shrines fill the view.

card.hook: Picture a hillside Thai house on stilts, tall trees all around, and a rose garden out front that looks like it belongs somewhere much cooler. That's Bhubing Palace, and it's a lovely place for a slow, green wander.
card.stand_here: Stand in the front gardens at Bhubing Palace, where you can see both the fountain and the palace buildings. Face the palace so the lawns and flower beds fill the bottom of your photo.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the palace and its leafy setting in one shot. Switch to 0.5x in the rose gardens to fit the flowerbeds and building together. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for roof edges and the stilts.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the palace on one of the third lines, and keep the roofline level with the top line.
card.best_time: Morning is usually the nicest, with cooler air and gentler light. The shade under the trees can be patchy at any hour, so check your screen before you move on.
card.selfie_here: Try the rose garden, standing among the flower beds, where the colour makes a bright backdrop. The water's edge by the reservoir in the grounds is another option, since the calm surface makes a peaceful background. Use the front camera, or 0.5x if you want more in the frame. Check your screen, because we can't promise the palace will be behind you at either spot.
card.rules_and_safety: The palace is open to the public except when the royal family is in residence, usually January to March, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot and one zoomed shot of the same view, with flowers in the foreground and the palace roofline on the top grid line.
card.good_to_know: Bhubing Palace was built in 1961 as a royal residence, and the mountain site was chosen for its cooler air. It's built in the central Thai ruean mu style (a group of houses) and stands on stilts, with the royal rooms upstairs and the entourage's rooms on the ground floor. Construction took five months, and the first royal guests were King Frederik IX and Queen Ingrid of Denmark in January 1962.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the front gardens at Bhubing Palace, where you can see both the fountain and the palace buildings. Face the palace so the lawns and flower beds fill the bottom of your photo.

card.hook: The name does the sales pitch here: Wat Chet Yot means 'seven-spired temple', and that's exactly the photo you're after. It's a windowless, flat-roofed building with a tall spire on top and smaller ones around it, and it looks like nothing else in Chiang Mai.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject, where the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Take the garden path to the front of the main chedi, then step back on the grounds until the whole building fits.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole chedi and the green grounds in one shot. Then switch to 1x for a cleaner, less stretched view, and use 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the carved figures and the spires.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the tall central spire up with the middle vertical line so everything stands straight.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light on the carvings and fewer harsh shadows. Go early if you want a quieter garden.
card.selfie_here: Try the raised square terrace the main chedi stands on, under the frangipani trees. Use the front camera at 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the spired chedi over your shoulder. Check on site that the angle works, because it's hard to tell from the ground where the best spot is.
card.ask_someone: Stand at the front of the chedi, near the two small spires set forward on the front platform, and ask a passer-by to step back on the grounds and shoot towards you so the spires rise behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is allowed, but don't use flash inside the buildings. Take your shoes off before going into the viharn or inner chamber, and cover your shoulders and knees. Opening hours can vary, so check when you arrive. One guide suggests visiting in the morning or afternoon rather than close to evening, so you can explore without rushing.
card.challenge: Walk all the way round the base and find the devas that look best from each side. Then take one photo of your favourite with the spires rising above it.
card.good_to_know: King Tilokarat commissioned the temple in 1455, after sending monks to Bagan to study the Mahabodhi Temple. The design looks to India for its inspiration. The walls carry about 70 stucco reliefs of devas (divine beings), some of them quite weathered.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the subject, where the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Take the garden path to the front of the main chedi, then step back on the grounds until the whole building fits.

card.hook: This building used to be a courthouse, so you can take your time: nobody's going to rush you out of the frame. The whole façade is the star, and you don't need a long walk to get it.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Lanna Folklife Museum itself, right where the phone icon sits on the map, and face the front of the building. Step back a little from the entrance so more of it fits in.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole building. If you can't step back far enough, try 0.5x, then use 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for roof edges and windows.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the walls up with the vertical lines so the building doesn't lean, then tap the building and slide a bit darker if the sky is bright.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon gives softer light on the façade. Midday sun can look harsh and flat.
card.selfie_here: Head to the open paved square at the Three Kings Monument, across Prapokklao Road from the museum, and turn so the museum is behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more building in, and check the view on your screen before you tap.
card.ask_someone: You stand on the Three Kings Monument square with the museum behind you, and ask a passer-by to stand on the same square, across from you, so the museum fills the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Outside photos are generally fine. Inside, flash isn't allowed and some halls prohibit photos, so look for signs and check the official site before you go. Don't pose irreverently with Buddha images, as the guide says that's a legal offense in Thailand. At the monument, shoot from the square, respect people making offerings, and don't climb it.
card.challenge: Take one straight-on shot of the whole façade, then find a doorway, roof edge or window and make it your close-up.
card.good_to_know: The building once belonged to the eighth ruler of Chiang Mai, Chao Intavaroros Suriyavongse. From 1935 it served as the Provincial Courthouse, and it was later renovated as a museum, which opened in 2012. Inside you'll find Lanna traditions, Buddhist art, ceremonial utensils, lacquerware, woven basketry and pottery.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the Lanna Folklife Museum itself, right where the phone icon sits on the map, and face the front of the building. Step back a little from the entrance so more of it fits in.

card.hook: Picture a square tower stepped up in five tiers, a big stone lion on every corner and rows of little yellow Buddhas looking out from their niches. That's Wat Chedi Liam, and it's a quiet one, so you can take your time.
card.stand_here: Stand near Sheik Istana on the east bank of the Ping River and face across the water to the stupa. One visitor review suggests this spot, but check it on site, because we haven't confirmed exactly where it is.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so you get the tower, the sky and the river all in one shot. If you're far back, try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to fill the frame with the tower. Save zoom 0.5x for inside the temple grounds, where you can stand close and still fit the whole height.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, put the tower on one of the vertical lines and let the river fill the bottom third.
card.best_time: After dark is the star time, when the tower is lit up with the river in front of it. Dusk works too, while the sky still has some colour.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the open ground at the foot of the five-tiered chedi, with the tower behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x so the tall tower fits over your shoulder. It's not an official photo spot, just the natural place to pose.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working temple, so dress modestly and keep your distance from monks and anyone praying. Look for signs about where photos are allowed, and try not to pose with your back to a Buddha statue. One visitor was surrounded by temple dogs, so stay alert and bring water, as there are few amenities.
card.challenge: Get a photo with one of the corner lions in the foreground and the top of the tower behind it, then see if you can spot a Buddha in every niche.
card.good_to_know: The temple was first built around 1287, and its square, stepped tower shows Mon influence from the Haripunchai style. A Burmese trader renovated it in 1908, which is why much of the decoration looks Burmese and most of the Buddha images on the tower wear yellow instead of white. It's in the Wiang Kum Kam area, a fair way from the old walled city, so plan it as a separate trip.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Sheik Istana on the east bank of the Ping River and face across the water to the stupa. One visitor review suggests this spot, but check it on site, because we haven't confirmed exactly where it is.
